title: Open work inventory: what's open, what to save, what to drop

steps.path: Every repo, on this computer and on GitHub
steps.headline: What I counted: 161 cards, about 100 work folders, about 90 unfinished branches, 8 open non-bot pull requests.
steps.changed: Five reviewers checked every card and every branch against what is actually in the app today. Roughly half the work folders are finished and simply never removed. About a dozen are real unfinished work. A handful hold files that were never saved anywhere but this disk.
steps.notice: Six sessions are running right now (Android fixes, Pages, the test-suite rethink, mesh sync design, local models, analytics). Nothing below touches those. Full findings: docs/active/investigations/2026-11-08-work-inventory/ in this session's folder.

steps.path: The cards folder and the Work board
steps.headline: The cards are noticeably out of date: many say work is pending that already shipped, and many say done-nothing while work exists.
steps.changed: Examples: 14 closed cards still say 'waiting on Destin' or 'nothing shipped' though they shipped. #213 Android says 'Done: nothing yet' while 57 commits of fixes sit on its branch. #172 Electron upgrade is already done. #133 one-settings-screen is obsolete (the phone already uses the desktop's settings). 9 cards still say 'blocks release 1.3.2', which shipped Oct 21. 55 of 75 open cards have no priority. 28 of 50 work branches aren't linked from any card. The whole security program (merged Nov 1-7) has no card.
steps.notice: Two weeks of merged work (security hardening, buddy rebuild, outside-file comments, analytics, voice, the send-blocked fix, the freeze fixes) is merged but in no released version yet. The last release is 1.3.3 (Oct 23).

steps.page: Protect work that exists only on this computer
steps.intro: These are files no backup has. Losing this laptop or cleaning the wrong folder would lose them.

steps.path: worktrees/sessions/ (148, 163, cc-reliability, the three 29-* bench folders, persona, user-notify, narrow-screens)
steps.headline: Should I save the never-saved files now, by committing each onto its own branch and backing it up to GitHub?
steps.today: Some old work folders hold changes that were never committed. The biggest: about 1,800 lines of speed-test lab tools (card #148), a half-done crash-recovery wording fix (card #163), your answers on an old reliability review deck, and three unsaved CI plan docs.
steps.problem: They exist only on this disk. Cleanup tools, a disk failure or a mistaken delete would lose them, and the cards don't mention them.
steps.proposal: Commit each pile onto its own existing branch and push it. That is a backup, not a release. Nothing changes in the app. Then each pile gets decided on its card.

options.label: Save all piles
pros: Nothing can be lost while you decide.
Costs nothing. Branches can be deleted later.
cons: Adds a few more branches to GitHub until they're cleaned up.

options.label: Only the real work
options.summary: Save the speed lab, the crash-recovery fix and your deck answers. Throw away the rest (old screenshots, plan drafts later rewritten).
pros: Less clutter.
cons: A reviewer judged 'not worth keeping'. It might be wrong.

options.label: Don't save
pros: Nothing new on GitHub.
cons: They stay at risk. Next cleanup could delete them.

steps.page: Clean up what's finished or superseded
steps.intro: Leftovers make every new session's startup report long and confusing, and hide the work that matters.

steps.path: worktrees/sessions/ and GitHub branches in all five repos
steps.headline: Remove about 50 finished work folders and their branches, here and on GitHub?
steps.today: About 41 folders in the five repos hold work that's already in the app (merged, or the same change landed another way). 4 more are empty leftovers. The automatic cleaner skips them because they hold throwaway screenshots and temp files it can't be sure about.
steps.problem: Every session's startup report lists them as warnings, so real problems get buried. They also slow down tools that scan every folder.
steps.proposal: After saving anything from Q-1, delete the finished folders and their branches. I'd first double-check each one has nothing that isn't already in the app, and skip anything a running session uses.

options.label: Remove them all
pros: Startup report shrinks to the work that matters.
Every one was checked: all of its content is already in the app.
cons: Old throwaway screenshots in them are gone for good.

options.label: Folders only
options.summary: Remove the folders on this computer but keep their branches on GitHub for a month.
pros: A safety net if a check was wrong.
cons: GitHub branch list stays cluttered. Needs a second pass later.

options.label: Leave them
pros: No risk at all.
cons: The clutter keeps growing (about 20 new leftovers in two weeks).

steps.surface: Branches with unique but outdated work
steps.path: Six CI speed experiments (29-*), release-1-3-2, the old roadmap and browser wrap-ups, the 1.3.1 dependency fix, an early copy of the Android branch, an older helper-plans copy, the sync-retry pull request
steps.headline: Drop these 14 branches whose work was replaced by something newer?
steps.today: Each has commits that aren't in the app, but a later change replaced every one. Examples: the CI experiments lost to a different approach that shipped (their pull requests are already closed). The release-1-3-2 notes were rewritten on master. The roadmap file they edit no longer exists.
steps.problem: They look like unfinished work in every report, so each new session wonders whether to rescue them.
steps.proposal: Delete them. A one-line note goes on the card each belongs to, saying what was dropped and why.
steps.risk: One judgement (the 1.3.1 dependency fix) is medium confidence: the files it changes are gone from the app, but I didn't confirm what replaced them.

options.label: Drop all 14
pros: Clears the most confusing leftovers.
Each was checked against what replaced it.
cons: Can't be brought back once deleted from GitHub.

options.label: Keep the doubtful one
pros: Keeps the one medium-confidence call for a closer look.
cons: One more leftover until someone checks it.

steps.path: ~/youcoded-dev itself, and the marketplace's shared copy
steps.headline: Move your personal files out of the YouCoded workspace and throw away stale leftovers there?
steps.today: The main folder holds: your Anthropic essay (.docx), flappy-bird.html (a copy already lives in ~/flappy-bird), about 10 empty 'Untitled' Word/Excel/PowerPoint files, and 141 MB of old landing-page screenshots. The marketplace's shared copy has 5 edited files that are older drafts of what's already on GitHub.
steps.problem: Personal files in a project folder risk being committed to a public repo by mistake. The stale edits block that shared copy from updating.
steps.proposal: Move the essay to ~/Documents. Leave ~/flappy-bird as the only copy of flappy-bird. Delete the empty Untitled files, the old screenshots and the 5 stale marketplace edits. I'd check each Untitled file is truly empty first.

options.label: Do all of it
pros: Nothing personal can leak into a public repo.
The shared copies can update again.
cons: If an Untitled file had something you wanted, it moves to the trash rather than staying put.

options.label: Move, don't delete
options.summary: Move everything into one folder (~/Documents/youcoded-dev-leftovers) and you sort it later.
pros: Nothing is destroyed.
cons: You end up sorting it yourself.

steps.path: Dependabot pull requests in four repos
steps.headline: Land the six safe automatic library updates, close the two broken ones, and give the risky three to the release workstream?
steps.today: GitHub's bot opened 12 update requests. Six pass all checks and change little (#701 Android build tools, #334-336 promo-video tools, marketplace #119 server tools, themes #39). Two are stale and failing (#466, marketplace #89, both a test-tool major version). Three are big jumps that fail Android or app tests (#702, #703, #714). Marketplace #115 fails a version check.
steps.problem: Open update requests pile up and hide security fixes. The big ones can break the Android app if merged carelessly.
steps.proposal: Land the six green ones, close the two dead ones, and make the three big ones plus #115 a task in the release workstream (page 5).

options.label: Yes, as described
pros: Six fewer open items, all passing their checks.
Risky ones get done carefully, not rushed.
cons: Landing even small updates changes what the next release contains.

options.label: All in the release
pros: Every change lands together and is tested once.
cons: They sit open longer.

steps.page: Small finished work waiting on your word
steps.intro: These are done or nearly done. Each needs a land-it or drop-it.

steps.path: Several repos
steps.headline: Which of these small, finished pieces should be landed? Unpicked ones get closed with a note on their card.
steps.today: Each is finished, small and checked by its session, but was never landed because landing waits on your word.
steps.problem: Finished work rots: every day it falls further behind and gets harder to land. Some of it, like your Nov 1 rule, is something you already decided.
steps.proposal: Pick the ones to land. I'd update each, re-run its checks, land it and clean up its branch and card.

options.label: One-branch rule
options.summary: Your Nov 1 rule ('one workstream = one branch per repo'; helpers commit onto it, never onto their own) into the main rules.
pros: Supervisors need exactly this rule. It's your own decision, and it never landed.
cons: None found.

options.label: Nightly test fixes
options.summary: Fixes 3 failing overnight tests. No change to the app.
pros: Your rule is failing tests get fixed when found.
cons: None found. It lands cleanly.

options.label: Keychain wording
options.summary: When a Linux computer has no secure password store, the app says so instead of 'helper could not start'.
pros: Honest error, per the error-message standard.
cons: Tiny user-visible wording change.

options.label: Analytics phone fix
options.summary: Phones on 1.3.1-1.3.3 were counted as Linux computers in your stats. Fixed in three repos.
pros: Your user numbers become right.
cons: Past charts shift when phones move to the Android column.

options.label: Crash recovery wording
options.summary: After a crash, a tool step that was interrupted says 'may have run' instead of 'canceled' (card #163, half done, needs a hand merge).
pros: Stops the app claiming something didn't happen when it may have.
cons: Needs about an hour to update and test.

options.label: Two record PRs
options.summary: Workspace PRs #267 and #271: records of the freeze work and the Windows fixes. Both cards already closed.
pros: Closes two stale pull requests.
Keeps the record.
cons: Docs only, so landing them changes nothing in the app.

options.label: Sync plan docs
options.summary: The 'slim synced chats' plan and the sync rethink brief. Docs only, inputs to the sync workstream.
pros: Sync supervisor starts from them on master instead of a side branch.
cons: Docs only.

steps.path: Workspace pull request #272 (card #29)
steps.headline: Close the faster-checks-for-card-only-changes experiment (pull request #272)?
steps.today: An experiment to make GitHub's checks finish faster when a change touches only cards. Its checks pass, but the script it changes no longer exists on master.
steps.problem: Landing it means rewriting it against today's tools, and card #29 has bigger CI work queued.
steps.proposal: Close it and leave a note on #29. The release workstream can redo it if speed still matters.

options.label: Close it
pros: One less stale item.
The idea stays on card #29.
cons: Card-only changes keep their current check time.

options.label: Redo it
pros: Faster checks on every card change.
cons: About half a day of work for a modest gain.

steps.page: Big unfinished projects that went stale
steps.intro: Three large builds fell 1,700-2,600 changes behind the app. Reviving each means rewriting a lot of it.

steps.path: Card #74 (approve a multi-step job up front), branch with 140 commits
steps.headline: Helper plans was built but is now very stale. Shelve it, revive it, or rebuild it fresh later?
steps.today: A full version (the assistant proposes a step-by-step plan that you approve before helpers run it) was built in September: 34,000 lines on its own branch. The app moved on 1,705 changes since. 40 places conflict. Its review deck was never answered. A separate branch holds the only copy of your decision record for it (506 files).
steps.problem: Reviving means days of untangling the chat engine's core, and the design may no longer fit. Leaving it means the card claims more progress than exists.
steps.proposal: Shelve: land the decision record onto master as a doc (so it's never lost), keep one snapshot branch, delete the other copies, and mark card #74 'explore, design reference exists'.

options.label: Shelve with record
pros: Your decisions are safe on master.
No multi-day rebase on a feature nobody's waiting for.
cons: When you want it, it's mostly a rebuild using the old design as a guide.

options.label: Revive it now
pros: Keeps the work already done.
cons: Several days, high risk to the chat engine, and the design must be reviewed again.

options.label: Drop it entirely
pros: Cleanest.
cons: Loses your decision record.

steps.path: Card #75 (choose skills and tools per project), app pull request #571, workspace #203
steps.headline: Per-project skills and tools was nearly done but is now very stale. Rebuild on today's app, or close it?
steps.today: A per-project switchboard for which skills and tools the assistant uses was built, with design decisions and a contract, and was 'awaiting UI review'. It's now 1,788 changes behind with 22 conflicts. The security work since then rewrote how plugins install.
steps.problem: Card #75 says 'human polish and review', but the branch can't be reviewed or landed as it is.
steps.proposal: Rebuild it on today's app, using its approved decisions and contract as the spec, inside the 'Projects, skills and Claude Code' workstream. Close the two old pull requests once the rebuild starts.

options.label: Rebuild from spec
pros: Your approved decisions carry over.
Fits the new plugin safety work instead of fighting it.
cons: One to two days of agent work plus a fresh look-over by you.

options.label: Untangle old branch
pros: Keeps more of the original code.
cons: Probably slower than rebuilding, and riskier around plugin safety.

options.label: Close it
pros: Cleanest.
cons: A feature you approved disappears.

steps.path: App pull request #476 (OneDrive) and card #155 (Google files)
steps.headline: Close the paused OneDrive fix (keeping a card for it), and keep Google files paused until its decision?
steps.today: OneDrive: a Windows-only fix for freezes when browsing OneDrive folders, paused with two known breakages (content search and folder watching turned off). It's 2,598 changes behind and no card tracks it. Google files: paused on purpose, waiting on your choice of building our own Google sign-in or using an existing tool (rclone).
steps.problem: Neither can be finished as it is. The OneDrive freeze still affects Windows users.
steps.proposal: OneDrive: write a card describing the freeze and the earlier attempt, then close the pull requests and delete the branches. Google: leave as it is. The connected-accounts workstream will ask you its question.

options.label: Yes, as described
pros: The Windows problem stays tracked.
Two dead pull requests go away.
cons: The old OneDrive code becomes a reference only.

options.label: Keep OneDrive open
pros: Nothing deleted.
cons: Keeps falling further behind.

steps.surface: Approved designs that were never built
steps.path: Branches: user-notify, narrow-screen-proposals, persona-prompt-eval, usage-visibility, dev-xray-tools, offline-auth, command-center concepts, model-picker-tags
steps.headline: Move your answered design decks onto master and give each design a card, then delete its branch?
steps.today: Eight designs got your answers on decks but were never built. Examples: the assistant notifying you when it needs you, the phone and narrow-window layout, a better assistant persona prompt, usage stats, X-ray dev tools. Your answers live only on side branches, and most have no card.
steps.problem: This is the most common way work goes missing here: a design gets approved, the session ends, and nothing points to it again.
steps.proposal: Copy each design's docs and your answers onto master, write or update a card for each (so it shows up on the Work board), then delete the branch. The relevant workstream picks it up.

options.label: Yes, card them all
pros: None of your decisions get lost.
Each appears on the Work board.
cons: About 6 more cards in the backlog.

options.label: Ask me per design
pros: You can drop ones you've changed your mind on.

steps.path: Google Ads beginner experiment plan, and the marketing-ads branch
steps.headline: Is the Google Ads experiment YouCoded work that belongs here with a card, or its own project?
steps.today: A plan for a beginner Google Ads experiment sits unsaved in the workspace, and an older marketing-ads branch exists. Neither has a card.
steps.problem: The workspace rule says only YouCoded work lives here. Ads to grow YouCoded is a gray area.

options.label: YouCoded, card it
pros: It's growth for the app, like the website, which lives here.
Shows up on the Work board.

options.label: Its own project
pros: Keeps the dev workspace about building the app.

steps.intro: So the Work board tells the truth, and supervisors start from accurate cards.

steps.path: cards/ and the Work board
steps.headline: Correct every card that's factually wrong today, in one pass?
steps.today: See the second card on page 1. Shipped work is described as pending, and pending work as not started. 9 cards have labels for releases that already happened. Some links point to docs or branches that don't exist. Some cards repeat the same 'chat started' line 77 times.
steps.problem: You and every agent read these cards to decide what to do next. Wrong cards waste sessions and hide real problems.
steps.proposal: One pass that fixes only facts. It rewrites stale progress lines, closes cards that are truly done (#172 Electron), marks #133 obsolete, removes dead release and blocker labels, trims repeated lines, fixes dead links, and links every live branch to its card. No priorities or groupings change in this pass.

options.label: Fix the facts
pros: The Work board becomes trustworthy.
Every change has evidence (a commit or pull request) in the findings.
cons: Many cards change at once. Your 'Changed since' view will light up.

options.label: Show me first
pros: You see every edit before it lands.
cons: A long list to read. Most edits are mechanical.

steps.path: cards/
steps.headline: Which card reorganizations do you want?
steps.today: Several cards are grab-bags ('five small faults', 'eight follow-ups'). Some cover the same thing twice, and a few aren't YouCoded work at all.
steps.problem: A grab-bag can never be closed, so it lingers. Duplicates split progress across two places.
steps.proposal: Pick any. Each is done with a one-line note on the affected cards.

options.label: Merge duplicates
options.summary: One 'dev copies of the app never touch the real one' card from #17, #218 and bits of #19 and #127. Also #188 into #184, #149 with #150, and the sync trio #121/#125/#127.
pros: One place per problem.
cons: Card numbers you remember will point to a merged card.

options.label: Split grab-bags
options.summary: Split #45 (a small Gemma licence notice vs a big downloader rewrite), #52 (assistant searches the marketplace vs parked ideas), #29 (CI speed vs release method vs build upkeep) and similar.
pros: Small parts can actually close.
Easier to hand to a supervisor.
cons: More cards in total.

options.label: Move non-YouCoded out
options.summary: #82 (share your Z13 tablet kit) gets its own project. #27 and the company-paperwork half of #31 go to the legal notes in your brain.
pros: Follows your Oct 24 rule: only YouCoded work lives here.
cons: They leave the Work board.

options.label: Security umbrella card
options.summary: One card for the security program, recording what shipped Nov 1-7 and linking its leftovers (#161, #216, #217, #219, #221, #223, #124).
pros: The biggest recent work gets a record and a home for what's left.
cons: None found.

options.label: Re-test 'probably fixed'
options.summary: About 10 cards describe bugs that look already fixed (#4, #7, #10, #11, #34, #35, #43, #66, #99, #101). An agent re-tests each in a dev copy and closes what's gone.
pros: Could close a big chunk of the backlog.

steps.path: Priorities on cards
steps.headline: 55 open cards have no priority. Should I propose priorities for every card on a deck you approve?
steps.today: Every card from #147 up has no P1/P2/P3. Some older P1s were deferred but still say P1 (#33, #60, #77).
steps.problem: Supervisors need to know what matters most in their area. Without priorities they guess.
steps.proposal: Yes means I draft a priority for every open card with a one-line reason, and you approve or change them on a follow-up deck. No leaves priorities as they are.

options.label: Draft, I approve
pros: Your call, with the legwork done.
cons: One more deck to answer (about 75 quick rows).

options.label: Supervisors decide
options.summary: Each supervisor proposes priorities for its own area when it starts.
pros: Spread out, with more context per area.
cons: No single view across areas.

steps.intro: Grouping the remaining work into areas one supervisor (with many helpers) could own end to end.

steps.path: How cards get grouped
steps.headline: How should a workstream be recorded, so a supervisor knows exactly what it owns?
steps.today: Cards have tags and an area, but nothing says 'these 12 cards are one job for one supervisor'. Overlapping tags mean one card can look like it belongs to three areas.
steps.problem: Two supervisors could grab the same card, or a card belongs to no one and is never done.
steps.proposal: Pick how to record it.

options.label: A workstream field
options.summary: Each card gets one 'workstream:' line. Each workstream gets a short brief doc: goal, cards, branches, what done means, what needs you. The Work board can group by it.
pros: Each card has exactly one owner.
Cards keep their own history and numbers.
cons: Small change to the card tool and the Work board.

options.label: Parent cards
options.summary: One big card per workstream that lists its child cards.
pros: No tool change.
cons: Lists drift out of sync with the cards, the same problem we have now.

options.label: Merge into big cards
pros: Fewest cards.
cons: Loses each item's own progress and history. Grab-bags never close.

steps.proposal: Pick every grouping that looks right to you. Sizes: S about a day, M a few days, L about a week, XL more than a week of agent work.

steps.path: How a supervisor session works
steps.headline: Approve this way of running a supervisor?
steps.today: Today one session works one card. Large efforts (security: 12 branches) ended as piles of branches that needed combining before you could review them.
steps.problem: Without a fixed pattern, each supervisor invents its own, and you get surprise branches, surprise merges or work that's never reported.
steps.proposal: Each supervisor gets: its workstream brief and cards. One branch per repo, with all its helpers committing onto it. Strong (Opus) helpers do the building, and a fresh helper reviews each piece. It backs up to GitHub as it goes, updates its cards as each piece finishes, shows you decks only at real decision points, and never lands anything without your word. Its last report names one branch per repo and says what's done, what's verified and what needs you.

options.label: Approve as written
pros: Matches your existing rules (no merge without you, one branch).
One branch per area makes review easy.
cons: Big branches mean bigger reviews. A supervisor can still pause to land a finished part early if you say so.

options.label: Land in pieces
options.summary: Same, but the supervisor asks you to land each finished card separately instead of all at the end.
pros: Smaller, more frequent reviews.
Less risk of a giant branch going stale.
cons: More interruptions for you.

steps.path: How many run at once
steps.headline: How many supervisors should run at the same time to start?
steps.today: Six sessions are already running (Android, Pages, test rethink, mesh sync, local models, analytics).
steps.problem: More at once is faster, but they collide when two touch the same files, they use a lot of your plan's usage, and each produces decks for you to answer.
steps.proposal: Start with two or three areas that rarely touch the same code. Add more once the pattern works.

options.label: Two or three
options.summary: My picks: Phone and Android (continuing the running session), Release and tests (gets security fixes out), and Workspace tooling (makes the rest smoother).
pros: Low collision risk.
A manageable number of decks for you.
cons: Other areas wait a week or so.

options.label: Five or six
pros: Much faster across the board.
cons: Higher usage, more collisions, more decks at once.

options.label: One, as a trial
pros: Prove the pattern first.
cons: Slowest.

steps.path: This session
steps.headline: After you submit, should this session carry out every Yes above, then write the workstream briefs?
steps.today: Everything above is a proposal. Nothing has been changed, deleted or landed.
steps.problem: The cleanup and card fixes are mechanical and could take a few hours of agent work.
steps.proposal: Yes: I carry out your answers in this order: save at-risk work, clean up, land what you picked, fix cards, then write a brief for each approved workstream (goal, cards, branches, what done means). Then I hand you a ready-to-paste start message per supervisor. No: I stop after saving the findings.
steps.changed: This session carries out every Yes above in the order listed, then writes the workstream briefs.
steps.notice: You'll get one summary at the end and start messages for each supervisor.
